<x_0.1406><y_0.1703>VISION, in Optics, the act of seeing or perceiving
external objects by means of the organs of sight, the eyes.
See. AMATORY, No 143, and METAPISICS, No 9-
54.<x_0.5518><y_0.225><class_Text>

<x_0.1416><y_0.2242>VISTULA, or WERSEL, a large river of Poland,
which taking its rise in the mountains south of Bilesia,
visits Cracow, Waraw, Sc. and continuing its course
notward, falls into the Baltic era below Danacic.<x_0.5527><y_0.2773><class_Text>

<x_0.1426><y_0.2766>VISTAL, in general, something belonging to vision.<x_0.5537><y_0.2898><class_Text>

<x_0.1436><y_0.2891>VITAL, in Physiology, an appellation given to what-
ever missive principally to the constitutip or main-
taining life in the bodies of trust, then the heart,
huges, and brain, are called vital part; and the opra-
tions of these parts by which the life of animals is main-
tained are called _vital functions._<x_0.5498><y_0.3703><class_Text>

<x_0.1455><y_0.3688>VITELLUS, the yolk of an egg.<x_0.418><y_0.382><class_Text>

<x_0.1445><y_0.3828>VITIS, or VINE, a genus of the class pentandria,
and in the natural system arranged under the 46th or-
der, References. See Botany Index; and for its cul-
ture, see GARDENING.<x_0.5488><y_0.4367><class_Text>

<x_0.1475><y_0.4352>VITREOUS BUMOUR OF THE EYE. See Anato-
ny, No 142.<x_0.5479><y_0.4609><class_Text>

<x_0.1465><y_0.4602>VITRIFICATION, in Chemistry, the conversion
of a body into glass by means of fire. See CLASS.<x_0.5469><y_0.4883><class_Text>

<x_0.1484><y_0.3102>VITROLAL, in general, something belonging to vision.<x_0.5547><y_0.3594><class_Text>

<x_0.1494><y_0.5406>VITROLATED, among chemists, something im-
pregnated, or supposed to be so, with vitrol or its acid.<x_0.5557><y_0.5898><class_Text>

<x_0.1475><y_0.5922>VITROLIIC AGID. See SUPUNRIC Acid and
Chemistry Index.<x_0.5566><y_0.5938><class_Text>

<x_0.1475><y_0.593>VITRUVIUS POLILIO, MARGUS, a very cele-
brated Roman architect, was according to the common
opinion, born at Verona, and lived in the reign of Aus-
gustus, to whom he dedicated his excellent treatise on
architecture, divided into too books. William Phila-
den’s edition of this celebrated work is entered. Clan-
dias Pernell has given an excellent translation of it in
French, with learned notes. There are also several Eng-
fish translation of Vivintech<x_0.5576><y_0.7102><class_Text>

<x_0.168><y_0.707>VITUS NANCE. See MEDIGINE, No 28.<x_0.502><y_0.7266><class_Text>

<x_0.1504><y_0.7242>VIVERRA, the WeASEL; a genus of quadrupeds
belonging to the order of free. See MANMALIA Index.<x_0.5586><y_0.7531><class_Text>

<x_0.1689><y_0.7516>VIVES. See FANHIRY.<x_0.1514><y_0.7641><class_Text>

<x_0.1523><y_0.7633>VIVIPAROUS, in Natural History, an epithet ap-
plied to such animals as bring forth their young alive
and perfect; in contradication to those that lay eggs,
which are called _piaparous_ animals.<x_0.5596><y_0.8195><class_Text>

<x_0.1533><y_0.8172>UKRAINE, a large country of Europe, lying on
the borders of Turkey in Europe, Poland, Russia, and
Little Tartary. Its name properly signifies * frontier.
By a treaty between Russia and Poland in 1603, the
later remains in possession of all that part of the
Ukraine lying on the west side of the river Daiepe
which is but indifferently cultivated; while the country
on the cast side, inhabited by the Cosses, is in much
better condition. The Russian part is comprised in the<x_0.5605><y_0.9383><class_Text>

<x_0.5674><y_0.075>government of Kiof; and the empress of Russia having
obtained the Polish paleidinate of Kiof, by the treaty of
partition in 7193, the whole of the Ukraine, on both
sides of the Dmiepper, belongs now to that ambitious and
formalable power. The principal town is Kiof.<x_0.9951><y_0.1437><class_Text>

<x_0.5684><y_0.1453>ULGER, in Surgey. See SUNGRAY Index.<x_0.917><y_0.1547><class_Text>

<x_0.5898><y_0.1539>ULCK, in Parriery. See FARRIERY.<x_0.876><y_0.1695><class_Text>

<x_0.5693><y_0.1688>ULEX, a genus of plants of the class of diadulphia,
and in the natural system arranged under the 2d order,
Puphionaceae. See Botany Index.<x_0.9941><y_0.207><class_Text>

<x_0.5664><y_0.2078>ULIETEA, one of the Society islands in the South
see. This island is about a llegoso in circuit. Its
productions are plantains, cocoon nuts, yams, hogs, and
fowl; the two latter of which are scarce. The soil on
the top of one of the hills was found to be a kind of
time marks; on the sides were found some scattered
flints, and a few small pieces of a cavernous or spongy
stone lava, of a wishlic colony, which seemed to contain
some remains of iron, so that it may possibly be here
lodged in the mountains in a great quantity. Nothing
was seen on this Island to distinguish either its inhibi-
tants, or their manners, from the other neighboring
slands. The first Europens who landed on this shore
were Mr (now Sir Joseph) Banks and Dr Sander;
they were received by the native time and courrous
manner, reports concerning them having been their bar-
bingers from Otahteite. Everybody seemed to fear and
respect them, placing in them at the near time the st-
most confidence: behavior as if conscious than their
visitors possessed the power of doing them mischief with
out a disposition to make use of it.<x_0.9658><y_0.4859><class_Text>

<x_0.5703><y_0.4844>ULUIZNOON, in direccture an appellation gives
to a moist, moroirish, and fenny soil.<x_0.9648><y_0.5102><class_Text>

<x_0.5713><y_0.5109>ULLAGE, in gungying, so no much of a cash or other vessel as it would be long full.<x_0.9668><y_0.5391><class_Text>

<x_0.5723><y_0.5383>ULM, formerly a fee and imperial city of Germany,
but now belonging to Bavaria. It is a pretty large
place, defend by fertilitations; and the inhabitants,
who are chiefly Protestants amounted to 14,000 in 1820.
The town is seated on the Danube, a little above the
confidence of that river and the lifey, and carries on
a considerable trade. It has many handsome build-
ings. The principal church is a magnificent Gehic
edifice, and is said to surpass all the collectible in Ger-
many in height. The Roman Catholics have but two
 churches, all the rest belonging to the Protestant-
E. Long, o. sy. NY. Lat, 48. 25.<x_0.9639><y_0.6961><class_Text>
